stem: Describe how collectivisation was carried out.

points.description: From late 1929 peasants forced to join collective farms, handing over land, animals and tools.
Collectives delivered fixed grain quotas to the state at low prices; machinery from Machine Tractor Stations.
Resisters labelled kulaks: property seized, many shot or deported (about 1.8 million deported, estimate).
Slowed briefly in March 1930, then resumed; about nine-tenths collectivised by the mid-1930s.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: From late 1929 peasants were forced to join collective farms, handing over their land, animals and tools. The collectives had to deliver fixed quotas of grain to the state at low prices and received machinery from Machine Tractor Stations. Peasants who resisted were labelled kulaks: their property was seized, and many were shot or deported, historians estimate about 1.8 million people in 1930-31. Stalin slowed the campaign briefly in March 1930, but pressure resumed, and by the mid-1930s about nine-tenths of households were collectivised.

stem: Explain why Stalin introduced the Five-Year Plans.

points.description: Identifies backwardness / fear of invasion.
Explains that he believed the USSR must catch up with the West quickly or be crushed, so heavy industry and arms were needed.
Identifies ideological and political aims.
Explains that industry would create a working class for socialism, end the NEP's private enterprise and increase state control.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Stalin believed the USSR was far behind the capitalist countries and must catch up within about ten years or be crushed by them, so it needed heavy industry and armaments quickly. Industrialisation also fitted communist ideas: it would create a large working class, the base of socialism, end the private enterprise of the NEP and give the state control of the whole economy.

stem: Explain how different groups in Soviet society were affected by Stalin's economic policies.

points.description: Identifies peasants.
Explains forced collectivisation, deportation of kulaks, low pay, restrictions on movement and the famine of 1932-33.
Identifies industrial workers.
Explains jobs and education but falling real wages, poor housing and harsh discipline (passports, penalties); Stakhanovites rewarded.
Identifies women or ethnic minorities.
Explains women's entry into work and the double burden, or minorities' Russification, deportations and the Kazakh famine.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Peasants suffered most: they were forced into collective farms, those labelled kulaks were deported, and collective farm members were poorly paid and could not leave; millions died in the famine of 1932-33. Industrial workers gained jobs, education and chances of promotion, but real wages fell in the early 1930s, housing was overcrowded and discipline harsh, with internal passports and penalties for lateness, although Stakhanovites earned bonuses. Women entered paid work in millions but still did most of the housework, a double burden, while ethnic minorities faced Russification and, in some cases, the deportation of whole peoples; Kazakh nomads were devastated by forced settlement.

explanation: Two marks per developed point (three groups).

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a table of the kind printed in Soviet official publications in the late 1930s (invented for this question)

> Electricity generated: 1928, about 5 billion kilowatt-hours; 1932, about 13 billion; 1937, about 36 billion.
> Pig iron produced: 1928, about 3 million tonnes; 1932, about 6 million tonnes; 1937, about 15 million tonnes.

**Source B** — a letter by a fictional American engineer working at a Soviet steel works, to his family, 1932 (invented for this question)

> The plant is enormous and the workers are young and keen. But half the machines we installed last spring are already broken through careless use, the barracks are freezing and the canteen serves the same soup every day. The managers report everything as done ahead of schedule. I have learned not to believe the figures on the factory noticeboard.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What does Source A show about Soviet industry between 1928 and 1937?

points.description: Output rose very fast between 1928 and 1937 (electricity about seven times, pig iron more than four times).
Growth continued through both plans and was largest in 1932-37 (e.g. electricity 13 to 36 billion kilowatt-hours).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How far does Source B support Source A?

points.description: Supports: huge new plants and keen workers suggest real growth.
Challenges: managers report everything as done ahead of schedule; figures not trustworthy.
Challenges: broken machines show waste and poor quality behind the numbers.
Adds: poor living conditions, which A does not show.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How useful are these sources for judging the success of the Five-Year Plans? Use the sources and your own knowledge.

points.description: A: useful for the scale of growth; historians accept growth was rapid.
A: official propaganda figures, some exaggerated; quantity, not quality or cost.
B: eyewitness from an outsider with no reason to praise; shows waste, false reporting, poor conditions.
B: one plant, one year (1932, the hardest year).
Own knowledge: new cities, industry moved east, consumer goods neglected, Gulag labour, famine.
Supported judgement on usefulness.

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.
One or two relevant but undeveloped points.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source A is useful because it shows the scale of growth in heavy industry, and historians accept that growth was very rapid even if some figures were exaggerated. But it is an official Soviet publication designed to show success, and it measures only quantity, saying nothing about quality, waste or human cost. Source B is useful because it comes from a foreign engineer with no reason to praise the system, and it reveals broken machines, false reporting and poor living conditions. However, it describes one plant in 1932, the hardest year. My own knowledge supports both: new cities such as Magnitogorsk and the move of industry east were real achievements, but consumer goods were neglected and forced labour was used. Together the sources are useful because each corrects the other: A shows what was achieved, B shows how and at what cost.

parts.explanation: Usefulness from content, provenance and own knowledge.

hints: Compare an official source with an eyewitness.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the main features of the Five-Year Plans.

points.description: Targets set by Gosplan for every industry and factory.
Concentration on heavy industry (coal, steel, oil, electricity, machinery), later armaments.
Huge projects (Magnitogorsk, Dnieper dam, Moscow Metro); industry moved east.
Harsh labour discipline, Stakhanovite movement and forced Gulag labour.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: 'Stalin's economic policies were a success.' How far do you agree?

points.description: Success: rapid growth of heavy industry; USSR a major industrial power by 1941
Success: industry moved east and armaments helped win the war; jobs, education and social mobility
Failure: collectivisation reduced output; livestock halved; famine of 1932-33 (estimates 5-7 million)
Failure: consumer goods and living standards neglected; waste, false figures, forced labour
Supported judgement

Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
In terms of Stalin's own aims, the policies were a success. Heavy industry grew very fast: official figures show coal production more than tripling between 1928 and 1937, and even allowing for exaggeration the USSR became a major industrial power by 1941. New cities such as Magnitogorsk were built, industry was moved east beyond the reach of invaders, and the armaments produced helped the USSR survive the German invasion. Unemployment disappeared and education spread.

However, the policies failed in other ways. Collectivisation reduced grain output in the early 1930s, livestock numbers fell by about half, and the famine of 1932-33 killed, by historians' estimates, about 5 to 7 million people. Consumer goods, housing and food were neglected, so living standards fell, and much production was wasteful, of poor quality or exaggerated. Much was built by forced labour.

I partly agree. The policies succeeded in making the USSR an industrial and military power and in giving Stalin control, but at an enormous human cost and with lasting damage to agriculture, so they cannot be called a success for the Soviet people.

parts.explanation: Levels: both sides with a supported judgement for the top level.

hints: In (b), judge success against Stalin's aims and against the cost to the people.
